596	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`, with the same
597	  404-before-422 precedence as the record list.
598	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests`
599	  — open a two-stage retention cleanup request for the version's masking-hit
600	  records. Body contains exactly `reason` and `before`:
601	  `{"reason": "legal hold expired", "before": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}`.
602	  `reason` must be a string that is non-empty after trimming whitespace;
603	  `before` must be an ISO-8601 date-time carrying a timezone (offset or `Z`),
604	  and a record belongs to the target set only when its hit write time is
605	  strictly earlier than that instant. Creating a request only returns a
606	  preview — no hit record is deleted or modified, and the record list,
607	  search, summary, diff, reconcile and trend responses stay unchanged.
608	  Returns `201` with `id`, `reason` (trimmed), `before` (echoed as
609	  submitted), `status` (`pending`), `created_at` and a `preview` block:
610	  `hit_count` (the number of records that would be cleaned up),
611	  `first_hit_at` / `last_hit_at` (the earliest and latest hit times in the
612	  target set, `null` when the set is empty) and `fields` (the distinct field
613	  names involved, sorted ascending; `[]` when empty). The target set is
614	  fixed at creation time: masking-hit records written afterwards never enter
615	  the request even when they precede the cutoff by clock time. At most one
616	  pending request may exist per version; creating another while one is open
617	  returns `409` and writes nothing (confirmed requests never block a new
618	  one). Unknown dataset/version → `404`; missing/non-string/blank `reason`,
619	  missing/unparseable/timezone-less `before`, an extra body field, a
620	  non-JSON/non-object body or any query parameter → `422` and nothing is
621	  written, with 404 taking precedence.
622	- `GET .../privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests` — list the
623	  version's cleanup requests sorted by request `id` ascending (empty when
624	  there are none). Confirmed requests stay listed and requests survive
625	  process restarts. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
626	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
627	- `POST .../privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests/{request_id}/confirm`
628	  — confirm a request with an empty request body and no query parameters.
629	  Confirmation atomically deletes exactly the target set frozen at creation
630	  and sets `status` to `confirmed`; the response is the request plus
631	  `confirmed_at` and `deleted_count` (the number of records actually
632	  deleted, possibly zero). Confirming an already-confirmed request returns
633	  `409` and never changes data again; concurrent confirmations have exactly
634	  one winner (the others get `409`) and can never leave the records half
635	  deleted. After a cleanup the surviving hit records keep their original
636	  `sequence` numbers and later hits continue the existing increasing run
637	  without reusing cleaned numbers; the record list and search return only
638	  surviving records, and summary, trend, diff and reconcile recompute from
639	  them. Access records are not cleaned up and the processing-task audit
640	  chain remains immutable. A request body or query parameter on the confirm
641	  endpoint → `422`; unknown dataset/version/request → `404` (precedence
642	  matches the hit-record reads), and confirming a confirmed request →
643	  `409`.
644	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/privacy-compliance-export` — read-only
645	  cross-version export of the dataset's whole privacy compliance state,
646	  computed fresh on every read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or
647	  deleted, and no hit record, access record or cleanup request is touched).
648	  The path carries only the dataset name; the request takes no body and no
649	  query parameters (`422`); an unknown dataset → `404`, with the same
650	  404-before-422 precedence as the hit-record reads. A dataset without
651	  schema versions returns `200` with an empty `versions` array and all-zero
652	  totals, never an error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
653	  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline):
654	
655	  ```json
656	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"policies":[...],"hit_count":0,"masked_count":1,"view_count":2,"cleanup_requests":[...]}],"totals":{...}}
657	  ```
658	
659	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
660	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry
661	  has exactly `version`, `policies`, `hit_count`, `masked_count`,
662	  `view_count`, `cleanup_requests` in that order. `policies` lists the
663	  version's registered policies ordered by policy id; each policy has `id`,
664	  `field`, `classification`, `masking`, `allowed_roles` and `enabled`.
665	  `cleanup_requests` lists the version's cleanup requests ordered by request
666	  id (both pending and confirmed are retained); each has `id`, `reason`,
667	  `status` and `created_at`. `hit_count` is the number of masking-hit
668	  records currently stored for the version, `masked_count` is the sum of the
669	  access records' masked-value counts and `view_count` is the number of
670	  access records; all three reflect the records surviving a confirmed
671	  cleanup. `totals` has exactly `policy_count`, `hit_count`, `masked_count`,
672	  `view_count` and `cleanup_request_count`, each the sum of the per-version
673	  values over the whole dataset.
674	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/privacy-policy-coverage` — read-only cross-version
675	  check of the dataset's privacy policy coverage, computed fresh on every
676	  read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or deleted, and no policy
677	  or identification record is touched). The path carries only the dataset
678	  name; the request takes no body and no query parameters (`422`); an
679	  unknown dataset → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
680	  compliance export. A dataset without schema versions returns `200` with an
681	  empty `versions` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON
682	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly
683	  one trailing newline):
684	
685	  ```json
686	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"fields":[...],"candidates":[...]}],"totals":{...}}
687	  ```
688	
689	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
690	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry
691	  has exactly `version`, `fields`, `candidates` in that order. `fields`
692	  lists every field of the version ordered by field name; each entry has
693	  `field`, `coverage`, `classification`, `masking` and `enabled`, where
694	  `coverage` is `enabled` (an enabled policy is registered), `disabled` (a
695	  policy is registered but disabled) or `unregistered` (no policy), and the
696	  last three keys report the registered policy's classification, masking and
697	  enabled state (all `null` when no policy is registered). `candidates`
698	  lists the advisory suggestions for fields that were identified with at
699	  least one name or sample hit but carry no privacy policy yet, ordered by
700	  identification record id ascending; each candidate has exactly `field`,
701	  `classification` and `masking`, and an identified field whose name and
702	  samples both missed does not appear. The candidates are a compliance
703	  self-check reference only: they never register a policy and never rewrite
704	  an identification record. `totals` has exactly `version_count`,
705	  `field_count`, `enabled_count`, `disabled_count`, `unregistered_count`
706	  and `candidate_count`, each the sum of the per-version values over the
707	  whole dataset.
708	
709	### Sensitive-field identification
710	
711	Sensitive-field identification produces candidate annotations for the fields of
712	a schema version. It complements the manual privacy policies but never creates
713	or modifies one: an identification is advisory only. Records (including their
714	stable ids) persist across restarts.
715	
716	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications` —
717	  identify one field. The body contains exactly `field` and `samples`:
718	  `{"field": "contact_email", "samples": ["alice@example.com"]}`. `field` must
719	  name an existing field of the version; its name and type are taken from the
720	  version definition. `samples` is an array of JSON scalars (strings, numbers,
721	  booleans or `null`) and may be empty; objects or arrays reject the whole
722	  request. The samples are never stored or echoed back. Returns the record;
723	  the first submission for a field returns `201`, re-running the same field
724	  refreshes the record in place (the id is unchanged) and returns `200`.
725	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications` —
726	  return every identification record of the version sorted by id ascending
727	  (empty when there are none). The endpoint takes no request body and no query
728	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
729	
730	  Each record has `id`, `field`, `field_type`, `evidence`, `confidence`,
731	  `source` and `created_at`. `source` references the identified field as
732	  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`. `evidence` is the ordered, de-duplicated
733	  list of hit kinds, name hits before sample hits:
734	
735	  - **Name hits** — the field name contains a sensitive word case-insensitively
736	    as a substring. The words are `email`, `phone`, `id_card`, `password`,
737	    `token` and `birth`, emitting `name:<word>` in that order.
738	  - **Sample hits** — only string sample values are inspected (numbers,
739	    booleans and `null` never hit), and only when the field's declared type is
740	    `string`; a field declared with any other type is matched by name alone,
741	    even when a sample looks like an email. `sample:email` requires exactly
742	    one `@` with non-empty text on both sides and a dot in the domain;
743	    `sample:phone` requires an 11-digit string starting with `1`. Either format
744	    matching is sufficient.
745	
746	  `confidence` is `high` when both the name and the samples hit, `medium` for
747	  samples only, `low` for the name only and `none` when neither side hits
748	  (`evidence` is then an empty list but the record is still generated).
749	
750	  One record is kept per field: a re-run overwrites the evidence and confidence
751	  in place with a stable id. Unknown dataset/version → `404`; a field that does
752	  not exist in the version → `404`; missing or extra body fields, a
753	  non-string or blank field name, a `samples` value that is not an array of
754	  scalars (objects and arrays included), an empty body, malformed JSON or any
755	  query parameter → `422` and nothing is written.
756	
757	#### Masking strategy suggestions
758	
759	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications/masking-suggestions`
760	  — read-only advisory masking-strategy candidates derived from the version's
761	  identification records. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
762	  parameters (`422` if either is present, with nothing written); unknown
763	  dataset/version → `404`. A version without identification records returns an
764	  empty list rather than an error.
765	
766	  Each candidate has exactly `field`, `classification`, `masking` and
767	  `allowed_roles`. Only records whose name or samples hit produce a candidate;
768	  a record with empty evidence is omitted. Candidates follow the identification
769	  records' `id` ascending and are recomputed on every read, so refreshing an
770	  identification changes the suggestion on the next request. The endpoint
771	  writes nothing, never registers a privacy policy and leaves the
772	  identification records' fields, ordering and refresh semantics untouched;
773	  the privacy view continues to mask according to registered policies only.
774	
775	  - `classification` is `PII` for email, phone, id-card and birthday hits, and
776	    `CREDENTIAL` for password and token hits. A field hitting both is `PII`.
777	  - `masking` reuses the privacy-view vocabulary: `partial` for `PII`
778	    candidates and `redact` for `CREDENTIAL` candidates (a both-kinds field
779	    takes `partial`); no new masking format is introduced.
780	  - `allowed_roles` is always an empty list: the suggested masking applies to
781	    every role, granting none an unmasked view.
782	
783	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications/masking-suggestions/register`
784	  — turn the current advisory candidates into registered privacy policies. The
785	  body contains only `{"fields": ["<field>", ...]}`: a non-empty array of
786	  distinct field names, each non-empty after trimming and naming an existing
787	  field of the version that currently has a masking suggestion candidate.
788	  Returns `201` with one privacy policy record per requested field, in the
789	  request's field-name order; each record has the same fields as the manual
790	  policy creation response (`id`, `field`, `classification`, `masking`,
791	  `allowed_roles`, `enabled`, `created_at`), is enabled by default and gets a
792	  service-generated id and timestamp. Each policy copies its candidate's
793	  `classification` and `masking` verbatim with the candidate's empty
794	  `allowed_roles`, so after registration every role sees those fields masked;
795	  the next privacy view read masks according to the new policies. The whole
796	  batch is validated before anything is written, so any rejection writes no
797	  policy and no timestamp. Unknown dataset/version, or a named field that does
798	  not exist in the version → `404`; a field without an available candidate
799	  (never identified, or whose identification record currently yields no
800	  candidate) or one that already has a privacy policy → `409`; two concurrent
801	  registrations of the same field leave exactly one winner. Missing or extra
802	  body fields, an empty `fields` array, duplicate, non-string or blank names,
803	  an empty body, a whitespace-only body, malformed JSON or any query parameter
804	  → `422` and nothing is written. Registration only reads the identification
805	  records and field definitions; it never writes or auto-refreshes an
806	  identification, and the read-only suggestions endpoint stays unchanged.
807	
808	### Row snapshots
809	
810	A row snapshot persistently records the rows of a schema version at one point in
811	time. Snapshots (including their rows) survive restarts.
812	
813	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots` — persist a snapshot.
814	  Body: `{"rows": [{...}, ...]}` where `rows` must be an array of JSON objects
815	  (it may be empty). The JSON values and the order of rows/object keys are deep
816	  copied verbatim. Returns `201` with `id`, `dataset`, `version`,
817	  `created_at` and `row_count` (no rows). Unknown dataset/version → `404`;
818	  malformed or non-object rows → `422` and nothing is written.
819	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots` — list snapshot
820	  metadata sorted by `id` ascending (no `rows`).
821	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}` — return
822	  the metadata together with the saved `rows`. Unknown dataset/version/snapshot
823	  → `404`.
824	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at?timestamp=<ISO-8601>` —
825	  return the most recent snapshot whose `created_at` is not later than
826	  `timestamp`, including its rows. The timestamp must be a timezone-aware
827	  ISO-8601 date-time (an offset or trailing `Z`): missing, invalid or
828	  timezone-less values return `422`; unknown dataset/version → `404`; when no
829	  snapshot exists at or before the timestamp the response is `404`.
830	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at/diff?from=<ISO-8601>&to=<ISO-8601>`
831	  — read-only time-travel row diff, appended one segment after the bare-row
832	  time lookup and accepting GET only. Each of `from` (the baseline) and `to`
833	  (the target) must be a timezone-aware ISO-8601 date-time; each side
834	  independently selects the latest snapshot whose `created_at` is not later
835	  than its own timestamp (the same selection as the bare-row lookup), so the
836	  two times may resolve to the same snapshot and a `to` earlier than `from` is
837	  valid — the two snapshots are simply compared in their named order. The
838	  comparison reads snapshots and rows and writes nothing. The JSON document
839	  is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
840	  newline) with top-level keys `from_timestamp`, `to_timestamp`,
841	  `from_snapshot_id`, `to_snapshot_id`, `added`, `removed`, `fields_added`
842	  and `fields_removed` in that order; the timestamps echo the submitted query
843	  values. `added` and `removed` use the exact comparison semantics of the
844	  snapshot-id diff (JSON-object multisets, key order irrelevant, array order
845	  and value types significant, duplicates counted; entries
846	  `{"row", "count"}` sorted by canonical row text). `fields_added` and
847	  `fields_removed` compare the top-level field names appearing on the
848	  snapshots' row objects: names only on the target side are added, names only
849	  on the baseline side are removed, names on both enter neither set, and each
850	  list sorts by field name ascending. When both times select the same
851	  snapshot all four collections are empty and the request succeeds. Unknown
852	  dataset/version → `404`, checked before every request-shape check; a missing,
853	  blank, repeated, unparseable or timezone-less `from`/`to`, an extra query
854	  parameter or any request body bytes (whitespace-only included) → `422`; a
855	  side with no snapshot at or before its timestamp → `404` and nothing is
856	  written.
857	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at/diff/masked` —
858	  role-masked time-travel row diff, appended one segment after the bare-row
859	  time diff and accepting POST only. The body contains exactly `role`,
860	  `from` and `to`: `{"role": "guest", "from": "<ISO-8601>", "to":
861	  "<ISO-8601>"}`; `role` must be non-empty after trimming and each time must
862	  be a timezone-aware ISO-8601 date-time (offset or `Z`). Each side
863	  independently selects the newest snapshot whose `created_at` is not later
864	  than its own timestamp, with exactly the same selection as the bare-row
865	  time lookup. Added and removed entries are first judged and counted from
866	  the raw, unmasked rows with the bare-row diff's JSON-object multiset
867	  semantics (key order irrelevant, array order and value types significant,
868	  duplicates counted): a row appearing several times stays one entry with
869	  its multiplicity, and masking only rewrites the entry's row data — entries
870	  are never merged or split. Entries sort by the canonical (key-sorted) JSON
871	  text of the raw row, so the output order is unaffected by masking. Each
872	  emitted row is then masked exactly as the row-submission privacy view masks
873	  it, applying only the version's currently enabled policies
874	  (`redact`/`partial` semantics, `allowed_roles`, nulls and uncovered fields
875	  behave identically). The response is the same deterministic document as
876	  the bare-row time diff (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
877	  trailing newline) with the same keys in the same order: `from_timestamp`,
878	  `to_timestamp`, `from_snapshot_id`, `to_snapshot_id`, `added`, `removed`,
879	  `fields_added` and `fields_removed`; the timestamps echo the submitted
880	  body values and the field-name sets carry no values, so masking can never
881	  change them. Every successful read appends one masking-hit record per
882	  value it actually masks, counted per occurrence across both snapshots'
883	  diff entries (an entry of count `n` whose covered value is masked yields
884	  `n` hit records; added-side entries first, then removed-side, each side in
885	  canonical row order), structurally identical to the regular view's hit
886	  records and continuing the same per-version sequence run, plus exactly one
887	  access record whose `row_count` is the total number of rows expanded from
888	  both sides' entries and whose `masked_count` equals the number of hit
889	  records the read wrote. The records enter all existing masking-hit/access
890	  reads, filters, summaries, diffs, reconciliation, trends and cleanup
891	  previews; records of one read share a write timestamp, sequences stay
892	  continuous across processes, and a write obstruction never fails the read.
893	  The read never modifies snapshots, rows, policies or identification
894	  records. Unknown dataset/version → `404`; each side with a usable
895	  timestamp is resolved independently, so a side with no snapshot at or
896	  before its timestamp is likewise `404` and precedes every shape check
897	  (including a missing or invalid timestamp on the other side); a missing or
898	  wrong-typed `role`/`from`/`to`, a role blank after trimming, an
899	  unparseable or timezone-less time, an extra body field, an empty,
900	  whitespace-only or non-JSON body, a non-object body and any query
901	  parameter are `422` and write nothing.
902	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at/masked-view` —
903	  role-masked time travel, appended one segment after the bare-row time
904	  lookup and accepting POST only. The body contains exactly `role` and
905	  `timestamp`: `{"role": "guest", "timestamp": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}`; the
906	  service selects the latest snapshot whose `created_at` is not later than
907	  `timestamp` (the same selection as the bare-row lookup). On success it
908	  returns `{"dataset", "version", "snapshot_id", "created_at", "rows"}`; the
909	  `rows` are an order-preserving copy of the snapshot's rows masked exactly
910	  as the row-submission privacy view masks them, applying only the version's
911	  currently enabled policies (`redact`/`partial` semantics, `allowed_roles`,
912	  nulls and uncovered fields behave identically). Every successful read
913	  appends one masking-hit record per value actually masked, structurally
914	  identical to the regular view's hit records and continuing the same
915	  per-version sequence run, plus exactly one access record whose
916	  `row_count` is the snapshot's row count and whose `masked_count` equals
917	  the number of hit records written by the read. An empty snapshot, an
918	  allowed role, all-null values and a version without policies all succeed
919	  and leave only the access record. The records enter all existing
920	  masking-hit/access reads, filters, summaries, diffs, reconciliation,
921	  trends and cleanup previews; records of one read share a write timestamp,
922	  sequences stay continuous across processes, and a write obstruction never
923	  fails the read. The read never modifies or deletes the snapshot or its
924	  rows and never changes policies or identification records. Unknown
925	  dataset/version → `404`, and no snapshot existing at or before the
926	  timestamp is likewise `404`, both checked before every shape check (the
927	  latter whenever the body carries a usable timestamp); a missing or
928	  wrong-typed `role`/`timestamp`, a role blank after trimming, an
929	  unparseable or timezone-less timestamp, an extra body field, an empty,
930	  whitespace-only or non-JSON body, a non-object body and any query
931	  parameter are `422` and write nothing.
932	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/diff/{other_snapshot_id}` —
933	  compare two snapshots as JSON-object multisets. Object key order does not
934	  affect equality, while array order and JSON value types do (e.g. `1`, `1.0`,
935	  `"1"` and `true` are all distinct), and duplicate rows are counted. Both
936	  snapshots must belong to the dataset and version named in the path, otherwise
937	  `422`; unknown dataset/version/snapshot → `404`. The response is
938	  `{"from_snapshot_id", "to_snapshot_id", "added", "removed"}`; `added` lists
939	  rows present more often (or only) in the `to` snapshot and `removed` the
940	  converse, each entry being `{"row": {...}, "count": <int>}` sorted by the
941	  canonical (key-sorted) JSON text of `row`.
942	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/snapshots/{base_snapshot_id}/diff/{target_snapshot_id}` —
943	  read-only comparison of two snapshots belonging to two **different** schema
944	  versions of the path dataset; the baseline snapshot is named first and the
945	  target second, and either version order is allowed. It takes no request
946	  body and no query parameters (`422`). Unknown dataset or snapshot → `404`,
947	  checked ahead of every request-shape check; a snapshot owned by another
948	  dataset, or two snapshots of the same schema version (same-version
949	  comparisons still go through the snapshot-id diff endpoint) → `422`. The
950	  JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace,
951	  exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `base_snapshot_id`,
952	  `base_version`, `target_snapshot_id`, `target_version`, `field_changes`,
953	  `added` and `removed` in that order. `field_changes` lists only additions,
954	  removals, type changes and nullability changes of the two versions' field
955	  definitions, reusing the compatibility/trajectory literals (`added`,
956	  `removed`, `type_changed`, `nullable_tightened`, `nullable_loosened`);
957	  several changes of one field collapse into a single entry (a type change
958	  wins over a nullability change), entries sort by field name and each entry
959	  has `field`, `kind`, `before` and `after`, with the missing side `null`
960	  (never omitted). Rows are projected onto exactly the field names defined
961	  in both versions — other stored keys and fields absent from a row do not
962	  participate — and the projections are compared with the same-version
963	  snapshot diff's multiset semantics (object key order irrelevant, array
964	  order and value types significant, duplicates counted). `added` lists
965	  rows present more often or only on the target side, `removed` the
966	  converse, each entry `{"row", "count"}` sorted by the canonical
967	  (key-sorted) JSON text of the projected row. The comparison is fully
968	  read-only: snapshots, rows, field definitions, the lineage impact cache
969	  and every privacy trail are never touched, and the result is identical
970	  across process restarts.
971	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/quality-rules/evaluate`
972	  — evaluate the version's enabled quality rules over the snapshot's persisted
973	  rows. The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`);
974	  unknown dataset/version/snapshot → `404` (checked first), and a snapshot
975	  owned by another version → `422`. The response and the rule semantics are
976	  exactly those of the row-submission evaluation (`{"dataset", "version",
977	  "results"}`), the snapshot and its rows are never modified, and every
978	  successful evaluation appends the same immutable history summary (with
979	  `row_count` set to the snapshot's actual row count) that also feeds the
980	  evaluation diff and anomaly detection. An empty snapshot is recorded with
981	  zero violations.
982	
983	### Retention policies and lineage-aware snapshot deletion
984	
985	A schema version can carry a single retention policy; snapshot deletion is a
986	two-stage request/confirm flow that refuses to remove snapshots still feeding
987	downstream fields. Policies and requests are persisted across restarts.
988	
989	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/retention-policies` — create the
990	  version's one retention policy. Body: `{"retention_days": 30}` with a
991	  non-negative integer. Returns `201` with `id`, `dataset`, `version`,
992	  `retention_days`, `created_at`. A second policy for the same version returns
993	  `409`; unknown dataset/version → `404`; other invalid input → `422`.
994	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/deletion-requests` —
995	  request deletion. Body contains only a non-empty `reason`. The snapshot and
996	  the version's retention policy must exist. Returns `201` with `id`,
997	  `snapshot_id`, `policy_id`, `reason`, `status`, `impacted`, `created_at`.
998	  `impacted` lists every field directly or indirectly reachable downstream of
999	  any field of the snapshot's version along lineage mappings; entries are
1000	  deduplicated and sorted by dataset, version and field ascending. The request
1001	  is `blocked` when any downstream field exists and `pending` otherwise. A
1002	  second `pending`/`blocked` request for the same snapshot returns `409`.
1003	- `GET .../snapshots/{snapshot_id}/deletion-requests` — list the snapshot's
1004	  deletion requests sorted by `id` ascending. The collection remains
1005	  addressable after a confirmed request has deleted its snapshot.
1006	- `POST .../snapshots/{snapshot_id}/deletion-requests/{request_id}/confirm` —
1007	  confirm a request (no body). Confirmation succeeds only while the request is
1008	  `pending` and the snapshot is at least `retention_days` old; otherwise `409`
1009	  and nothing is deleted. On success the snapshot is deleted atomically with
1010	  the status change to `confirmed`, and the response adds `confirmed_at`. Once
1011	  deleted, the snapshot no longer appears in snapshot read, list, `at` or diff
1012	  responses.
1013	
1014	  Unknown dataset/version/snapshot/policy/request → `404`; other invalid input
1015	  → `422` and nothing is written.
1016	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/retention-sweep` —
1017	  batch retention cleanup of the version's snapshots, appended one segment
1018	  after the version's snapshot collection and accepting POST only. The body
1019	  contains only a non-empty `reason`: `{"reason": "retention reached"}` (the
1020	  trimmed reason is stored on every request the sweep opens). Every snapshot
1021	  of the version is scanned in snapshot-id order: a snapshot whose age has
1022	  reached the version's retention days (the same age judgment as the
1023	  deletion-request confirmation) and that carries no open (`pending`/
1024	  `blocked`) deletion request gets a new request with the submitted reason —
1025	  `blocked` when the version feeds downstream fields and `pending` otherwise,
1026	  the same status judgment as the single-snapshot entry. A snapshot with an
1027	  open request is skipped (never duplicated, never modified) and a snapshot
1028	  younger than the retention age is skipped and only counted; a version
1029	  without snapshots sweeps successfully with empty collections. The whole
1030	  scan runs in a single transaction — either every new request is written or
1031	  none is — and concurrent sweeps of the same version have a single winner,
1032	  the loser receiving `409` and changing nothing. The response is a
1033	  deterministic JSON document (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly
1034	  one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`, `version`, `created`,
1035	  `skipped` and `counts` in that order. `created` and `skipped` are sorted by
1036	  snapshot id ascending; each entry has exactly `snapshot_id`, `request_id`,
1037	  `status` and `reason` (skipped entries echo the existing open request).
1038	  `counts` gives `created_count`, `skipped_count` and `not_due_count`, each
1039	  equal to the number of snapshots in that category. The opened requests are
1040	  ordinary deletion requests: they enter the existing deletion-request list
1041	  and confirm flow, are deleted atomically on confirmation and persist across
1042	  restarts. Unknown dataset/version → `404` (judged before every body/query
1043	  shape check); a version without a registered retention policy → `404`; a
1044	  missing, non-string or blank `reason`, an extra body field, an empty or
1045	  whitespace-only body, malformed JSON, a non-object body or any query
1046	  parameter → `422` and nothing is written.
1047	
1048	### Processing tasks
1049	
1050	A processing task is a named unit of work attached to a schema version; each
1051	run records one attempt. Tasks and runs are persisted across restarts.
1052	
1053	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks` — create a
1054	  task. Body: `{"name": "extract", "depends_on": [1], "max_attempts": 3}`.
1055	  `name` must be non-empty and unique within the version (`409` on conflict);
1056	  `depends_on` is an array of distinct task ids from the same version (default
1057	  `[]`, unknown ids → `404`); `max_attempts` is a positive integer (default
1058	  `1`). Returns `201` with `id`, `dataset`, `version`, `name`, `depends_on`,
1059	  `max_attempts`, `status` (`pending`), `attempt_count` (`0`) and
1060	  `created_at`. Other invalid input → `422` and nothing is written.
1061	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks` — list tasks
1062	  sorted by `id` ascending.
1063	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/{task_id}` —
1064	  return the task together with its `runs`, sorted by `attempt` ascending.
1065	  Each run has `id`, `task_id`, `attempt`, `status`, `started_at`,
1066	  `finished_at` and `error`. Unknown dataset/version/task → `404`.
1067	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/{task_id}/runs` —
1068	  start a new run. Only allowed while the task is `pending` or `failed`, has
1069	  attempts left (`attempt_count < max_attempts`) and every task in
1070	  `depends_on` has status `succeeded`; otherwise `409` and nothing is written.
1071	  Returns `201` with the new `running` run and increments the task's
1072	  `attempt_count` (the task becomes `running`).
1073	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/dispatch` —
1074	  worker batch claim. The body is optional and contains only an optional
1075	  `limit`: omit the body (or send `{}`) to claim one task, or send
1076	  `{"limit": <positive integer>}`. Within a single transaction, up to `limit`
1077	  startable tasks are selected by task id ascending; a task is startable when
1078	  it is `pending`, or `failed` with attempts left, and every direct dependency
1079	  is `succeeded` at selection time. Each selected task gets a new `running`
1080	  run for its next attempt, `attempt_count` is incremented and the task becomes
1081	  `running`. `running`, `succeeded`, attempt-exhausted and dependency-blocked
1082	  tasks are skipped; a task started earlier in the same request is only
1083	  `running`, so its dependents are not selectable until a later request.
1084	  Returns `201` with `{"dataset", "version", "runs"}`; `runs` is sorted by
1085	  task id ascending and each run has the same fields as the single-task start
1086	  endpoint. When no task is startable the response is still `201` with an
1087	  empty `runs` list. Concurrent dispatches (and dispatches interleaved with
1088	  single-task starts) never create a duplicate attempt or two running runs for
1089	  the same task, and a single response never exceeds `limit`. Unknown
1090	  dataset/version → `404`; extra body fields, a non-integer (including
1091	  boolean) or non-positive `limit` → `422` and nothing is written.
1092	- `PATCH /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/{task_id}/runs/{run_id}` —
1093	  finish the currently running run. Body: `{"status": "succeeded"}` or
1094	  `{"status": "failed", "error": "<non-empty message>"}`. Writes `finished_at`
1095	  and moves the task to the same status; a `failed` task with attempts left
1096	  can be started again. Finishing an already finished run → `409`; a run that
1097	  does not belong to the task/version in the path → `422`; unknown
1098	  dataset/version/task/run → `404`; other invalid input → `422` and nothing
1099	  is written.
1100	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/batch-complete` —
1101	  finish several currently running runs in one transaction. Body contains only
1102	  a non-empty `runs` array; each item names a task of the path version and one
1103	  of its runs: `{"task_id": <int>, "run_id": <int>, "status": "succeeded"}` or
1104	  the same with `"status": "failed"` and an `error` that is non-empty after
1105	  trimming whitespace (`succeeded` items carry no `error`). The same task must
1106	  not appear twice. The whole batch is validated before any write and either
1107	  every item completes or none do; on success the response is
1108	  `{"dataset", "version", "runs"}` with the completed runs sorted by task id
1109	  ascending, each carrying the same fields as the single-run finish response.
1110	  Every run gets a `finished_at` timestamp and its task moves atomically to
1111	  the same status; `failed` tasks keep their consumed attempts and stay
1112	  retryable while attempts remain. Tasks whose dependencies succeed in the
1113	  same batch are not started or skipped within that batch (the dependencies
1114	  are `running` at selection time, as with dispatch) and become startable
1115	  immediately afterwards, each at its next continuous attempt. Empty/missing
1116	  `runs`, extra fields, non-integer (including boolean) ids, an unknown status
1117	  or a missing/blank/non-string `error` → `422`; an empty body or malformed
1118	  JSON → `422`; any query parameter → `422`. Unknown dataset/version → `404`;
1119	  a batch task that does not exist or belongs to another dataset/version →
1120	  `404`; an unknown run → `404` (a run belonging to another dataset/version is
1121	  treated as out of scope); a run that belongs to another task of the same
1122	  version → `422`. An already finished run, a duplicate task in the batch or a
1123	  task that is not currently `running` (not currently completable) → `409`,
1124	  and the entire batch is rolled back: statuses, timestamps and counters are
1125	  unchanged. Concurrent batch completion is single-winner against the
1126	  single-run finish/cancel endpoints, run starts and batch dispatch: exactly
1127	  one racing operation commits and the others receive `409`, never leaving a
1128	  `running` run with a half-written `finished_at` or rolling `attempt_count`
1129	  back. Audit records appended afterwards record the run's terminal status,
1130	  and the schedule, audit report and post-restart reads present the batch
1131	  results through the existing fields and ordering.
1132	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/{task_id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel` —
1133	  cancel the currently running run. The body contains only a non-empty
1134	  `reason` string; leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed and the result
1135	  is stored as the run's `error`. Returns the updated run with `finished_at`
1136	  written and `status` `failed`; the task is atomically moved to `failed` in
1137	  the same transaction while `attempt_count` is not rolled back, so a
1138	  cancelled task follows the existing start rules: it can run again when its
1139	  dependencies have succeeded and attempts remain, and the next run keeps the
1140	  continuous attempt sequence. Only a `running` run can be cancelled;
1141	  cancelling an already `succeeded`/`failed` run returns `409` and changes no
1142	  field. A run that does not belong to the task/version in the path → `422`;
1143	  unknown dataset/version/task/run → `404`; a missing reason, an extra body
1144	  field, a non-string reason or one that is blank after trimming, an empty
1145	  body, malformed JSON or any query parameter → `422` and nothing is
1146	  written. Cancellation is single-winner against finishing, single-task
1147	  starts and batch dispatch: exactly one racing operation performs the state
1148	  transition and the others receive `409`, so no run is left `running` with a
1149	  half-written `finished_at`.
1150	- `PUT /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/{task_id}/dependencies` —
1151	  atomically replace the task's dependency list. Body contains only
1152	  `{"depends_on": [<task id>, ...]}` (the array may be empty); the ids must
1153	  reference existing tasks of the same version without duplicates and must not
1154	  include the target task itself. The replacement is rejected when the target
1155	  task is not `pending` or when it would introduce a cycle in the dependency
1156	  graph; on success the updated task is returned. Unknown
1157	  dataset/version/task/dependency → `404`; a self dependency, a cycle or a
1158	  non-`pending` target → `409`; any other invalid body → `422` and nothing is
1159	  written. The existing run-start rule uses the updated dependencies.
1160	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/schedule` —
1161	  return `{"dataset", "version", "tasks"}` with tasks sorted by `id` ascending.
1162	  Each task carries every processing-task field plus `schedule_state` and
1163	  `blocking_task_ids`. `schedule_state` is `running` or `succeeded` for tasks
1164	  in those states; a `failed` task is `retryable` while attempts remain and
1165	  `exhausted` once they are used up; a `pending` task is `ready` when all of
1166	  its direct dependencies have succeeded, `upstream_failed` when any
1167	  dependency chain contains an `exhausted` or `upstream_failed` task, and
1168	  `blocked` otherwise. `blocking_task_ids` lists the direct dependencies that
1169	  have not succeeded, sorted ascending; it is empty for non-pending tasks.
1170	  States are recomputed on every read (including after a successful retry)
1171	  and both the dependency graph and the schedule survive restarts.
1172	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/audit-report` —
1173	  read-only audit report for the whole version; the endpoint takes no request
1174	  body and no query parameters (both are rejected with `422`; unknown
1175	  dataset/version → `404`). Returns
1176	  `{"dataset", "version", "summary", "tasks"}`. `summary` contains
1177	  `task_count`, `run_count`, `pending_tasks`, `running_tasks`,
1178	  `succeeded_tasks`, `failed_tasks`, `exhausted_tasks` and
1179	  `invalid_audit_runs`; status counters count tasks by their stored status,
1180	  `exhausted_tasks` counts `failed` tasks that have used up
1181	  `max_attempts`, and `invalid_audit_runs` counts runs whose audit chain fails
1182	  re-verification. `tasks` is sorted by task `id` and each task carries every
1183	  processing-task field plus `runs`; `runs` is sorted by `attempt` and each
1184	  run carries its run fields plus `proof`. `proof` re-runs the same checks as
1185	  the per-run verify endpoint over that run's audit chain and is
1186	  `{"valid", "checked_count", "last_evidence_hash"}`; `last_evidence_hash` is
1187	  the stored evidence hash of the chain's final record and is `null` only for
1188	  an empty chain — it is still returned when `valid` is `false`, and the run
1189	  details are retained. Summary counters always agree with the returned
1190	  details and the report is deterministic across restarts.
1191	
1192	### Processing run audit records (append-only proof chain)
1193	
1194	Every run carries an independent, tamper-evident chain of audit records.
1195	Records are append-only (the database rejects updates and deletes, and there
1196	are no per-record HTTP routes), numbered from `1` per run and linked through
1197	SHA-256 evidence hashes. They persist across restarts.
1198	
1199	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/processing-tasks/{task_id}/runs/{run_id}/audit-records` —
1200	  append a record. Body contains exactly `event`, `input_summary` and
1201	  `result_summary`, each a string that is non-empty after trimming whitespace.
1202	  Returns `201` with the submitted fields plus `id`, `sequence` (continuous
1203	  from `1` within the run), `run_status` (the run's status at write time:
1204	  `running`/`succeeded`/`failed`), `previous_hash` (`null` for the first
1205	  record, otherwise the previous record's `evidence_hash`), `evidence_hash`
1206	  and `created_at`. Missing, extra, non-string or blank fields → `422` and
1207	  nothing is written; unknown dataset/version/task/run → `404`; a run that
1208	  does not belong to the path task (including one in another version) →
1209	  `422`. Concurrent appends never reuse a sequence or break the chain.
1210	- `GET .../runs/{run_id}/audit-records` — list the run's records in ascending
1211	  `sequence` order. Same `404`/`422` path rules.
1212	- `GET .../runs/{run_id}/audit-records/verify` — verify the chain. Returns the
1213	  path identifiers together with `valid` and `checked_count`:
1214	  `{"dataset", "version", "task_id", "run_id", "valid", "checked_count"}`.
1215	  Verification recomputes every `evidence_hash`, checks that `sequence` values
1216	  are continuous from `1` and that each `previous_hash` equals the preceding
1217	  record's `evidence_hash` (the first must be `null`). An intact chain returns
1218	  `"valid": true` (also for an empty chain).
1219	
1220	`evidence_hash` is the hexadecimal SHA-256 of a canonical JSON document built
1221	from every stored field except `id`, `created_at` and `evidence_hash` itself
1222	(`event`, `input_summary`, `result_summary`, `sequence`, `run_status`,
1223	`previous_hash`): keys are sorted by Unicode code point, no insignificant
1224	whitespace is emitted and the text is UTF-8 encoded.
1225

# Data Lineage Trust Platform

Backend service for managing datasets, their immutable schema versions and
field-level lineage between schema versions. All metadata is persisted in a
SQLite database, so data created before a restart remains queryable afterwards.

## Requirements

- Python 3.12+

## Install and test

```bash
python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
python -m pytest
```

## Start

```bash
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

The SQLite database is stored at `data/lineage.db` by default. Override the
location with the `DATA_LINEAGE_DB` environment variable.

## Public API

All endpoints return JSON. Error responses use the stable shape
`{"error": "<code>", "detail": "<message>"}` and never expose SQL or stack
traces.

### Health

- `GET /health` returns `{"status":"ok"}` when the service is ready.

### Datasets

- `POST /datasets` — create a dataset. Body: `{"name": "orders", "description": "optional"}`.
  Returns `201` with `id`, `name`, `description`, `created_at`. Empty name →
  `422`; duplicate name → `409`.
- `GET /datasets` — list all datasets.

### Schema versions (immutable, numbered from 1 per dataset)

- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions` — create the next schema version. Body:
  `{"fields": [{"name": "id", "type": "integer", "nullable": false}]}`.
  Field list must be non-empty, field `name`/`type`/`nullable` are required and
  field names must be unique within the version. Unknown dataset → `404`;
  invalid fields → `422` (nothing is written).
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions` — list all versions of a dataset with
  their fields.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}` — read one version with its
  fields. Unknown dataset/version → `404`.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{base_version}/compatibility/{target_version}` —
  read-only breaking-change check of the target version against the base
  version, computed fresh from the persisted field definitions on every read
  (nothing is written; field order is not a difference). The endpoint takes no
  request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version →
  `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the version diff. The JSON
  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
  trailing newline) with top-level keys `base_version`, `target_version`,
  `breaking_changes` and `breaking_change_count`. A breaking change is exactly
  one of: the target removed a base field (`removed`), changed a field's type
  (`type_changed`) or tightened a nullable field to not nullable
  (`nullable_tightened`); added fields and nullable loosening are not
  breaking. Each entry has `field`, `kind`, `before` (base definition) and
  `after` (target definition, `null` for a removed field), entries are sorted
  by field name ascending and `breaking_change_count` equals the number of
  entries. Comparing a version with itself returns an empty list and a zero
  count. The verdict is advisory for release decisions only: it runs no
  migration or rollback.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{base_version}/compatibility/{target_version}/impact` —
  read-only companion of the compatibility check: the same top-level keys
  (`base_version`, `target_version`, `breaking_changes`,
  `breaking_change_count`) and the same breaking entries, each entry carrying
  one extra key `impacted` after `after`. `impacted` lists every field
  directly or indirectly downstream of the broken field along the lineage
  mappings, starting from the base version's same-named field and — when the
  field still exists in the target version — also from the target version's
  field. Each item is `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`; the set is
  deduplicated, never contains a start field itself (cycles terminate) and is
  sorted by dataset, version and field ascending. A field with no downstream
  yields an empty list. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404` with the same
  404-before-422 precedence as the compatibility check, and the JSON document
  is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
  newline). The read is fully side-effect free: version definitions, lineage
  mappings and the impact cache are never written.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/evolution-summary` — read-only whole-dataset
  summary of adjacent-version breaking changes and their downstream impact,
  computed fresh on every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version
  definitions, lineage mappings and the impact cache are never touched).
  Quality and privacy state play no role. The path carries only the dataset
  name; the request takes no body and no query parameters (`422`); an unknown
  dataset → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
  compatibility reads. A dataset with fewer than two versions returns `200`
  with an empty `pairs` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON
  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
  trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`, `pairs` and `totals`.
  `pairs` is ordered by base version number ascending and lists every
  adjacent version pair, including pairs without breaking changes; each entry
  has exactly `base_version`, `target_version`, `breaking_count`,
  `impacted_count` and `impacted_datasets` in that order. `breaking_count` is
  the number of breaking entries of the pair, judged exactly as in the
  pairwise compatibility impact response (`removed`, `type_changed` or
  `nullable_tightened`; several changes of one field collapse into a single
  entry). The pair's impacted set is the union of every breaking entry's
  downstream fields — same start-field rule as the pairwise impact response,
  merged and deduplicated, never containing a start field itself (cycles
  terminate) — `impacted_count` is its size and `impacted_datasets` lists the
  distinct dataset names appearing in it, sorted ascending. `totals` has
  exactly `pair_count` (the number of pairs), `breaking_count` and
  `impacted_count`, each the sum of the per-pair values over the whole
  dataset.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/fields/{field}/trajectory` — read-only
  cross-version trajectory of one named field of the dataset, computed fresh
  on every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions,
  lineage mappings and the impact cache are never touched). Only the
  persisted version field definitions and lineage mappings are read; quality,
  privacy, snapshot and processing-task state play no role. The path carries
  the dataset name and the field name; the request takes no body and no query
  parameters (`422`); an unknown dataset → `404`, and a field that does not
  appear in any of the dataset's versions → `404`, both with the same
  404-before-422 precedence as the evolution summary. A dataset with fewer
  than two versions returns `200` with an empty `changes` array, never an
  error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact
  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`,
  `field`, `entries` and `changes` in that order. `entries` lists every
  schema version of the dataset ordered by version number ascending; each
  entry has exactly `version` and `definition`, where `definition` is the
  field's persisted definition in that version (`type` and `nullable` only)
  or `null` — the key is never omitted — when the field does not exist
  there. `changes` lists one entry per adjacent version pair, ordered by
  base version ascending; each entry has exactly `base_version`,
  `target_version`, `status`, `impacted` and `impacted_datasets` in that
  order. `status` reuses the breaking-entry vocabulary of the compatibility
  check — `added` (the field appears on the target side), `removed` (it
  disappears on the target side), `type_changed`, `nullable_tightened` —
  extended with `nullable_loosened` (only the nullability relaxes) and
  `unchanged` (both definitions agree, including both absent); a field that
  both changes type and tightens nullability collapses into a single
  `type_changed` status. `impacted` lists every field directly or indirectly
  downstream of the tracked field for that pair along the lineage mappings,
  with the same start-field rule as the pairwise compatibility impact
  response (the base version's same-named field and, when it exists, the
  target version's); each item is `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`, the set
  is deduplicated, never contains a start field itself (cycles terminate),
  is sorted by dataset, version and field ascending and is empty when the
  field has no downstream. `impacted_datasets` lists the distinct dataset
  names appearing in `impacted`, sorted ascending.

### Field-level lineage

A lineage link maps one field of a target schema version to one field of a
schema version in a different (source) dataset.

- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — register a mapping.
  Body names both ends:

  ```json
  {
    "target_dataset": "dm_orders",
    "target_version": 1,
    "target_field": "id",
    "source_dataset": "raw_orders",
    "source_version": 1,
    "source_field": "order_id"
  }
  ```

  Target must match the path. Source and target datasets must differ and every
  referenced dataset/version/field must exist (`404` / `422` otherwise).
  Submitting the same complete mapping twice returns `409`.
- `DELETE /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — remove one
  registered mapping. Same address and same body shape as registration: the
  six locating fields name the complete mapping to delete and the body target
  must match the path. Every locating value readable in the request is
  resolved first, so an unknown dataset, version or field is a `404` ahead of
  every request-shape error; when all six values name existing resources but
  the mapping itself was never registered, the delete is likewise a `404`.
  An empty or whitespace body, invalid JSON, a non-object payload, missing or
  extra fields, wrongly typed values, blank names, any query parameter, a
  mapping whose source and target datasets coincide or whose body target
  disagrees with the path are all `422`. No rejection changes the lineage
  graph, the impact cache or any other metadata. A registered mapping is
  deleted atomically and returns `200` with the removed mapping in the
  registration response shape; concurrent deletes of the same mapping succeed
  exactly once (the loser gets `404` and changes nothing). The deletion is
  visible to every lineage read immediately and survives restarts; the cached
  impacts of the mapping's source field and of every field that can reach it
  are invalidated exactly as on registration, unrelated entries are kept.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — return every target
  field (including fields without sources) together with its source references.
  Results are sorted by target field name, then source dataset name, source
  version and source field name.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact?field=<field>` —
  return the downstream impact of one source field. The path and the `field`
  query parameter together name an existing field; the response is
  `{"source": {...}, "impacted": [...]}` where `impacted` lists every field
  reachable from the source along lineage mappings (direct and indirect), each
  entry being `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`. Results are deduplicated,
  never contain the source itself (cycles terminate) and are sorted by dataset,
  version and field ascending. Unknown dataset/version/field → `404`; a
  missing, blank, invalid or repeated `field` parameter → `422` (a repeated
  `field` is judged before the field lookup, so it is always a `422`, never a
  field `404`).
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-audit` —
  read-only consistency audit of the version's impact cache, appended one
  segment after the impact query address. The path dataset and version name
  the audit scope; every field of that version is checked against its current
  cache record and recomputed fresh from the committed lineage graph using
  exactly the impact-query semantics (downstream fields merged and
  deduplicated, the start field excluded, cycles terminating). Each entry is
  `{"field", "status"}` with `cached` (the stored record equals the
  recomputed result), `missing` (no cache record because the field's impact
  was never queried — a normal state, not an error) or `mismatch` (the stored
  record differs). Entries are sorted by field name ascending and the sort
  does not depend on database order. The JSON document is deterministic
  (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with
  top-level keys `dataset`, `version`, `entries` and `counts` in that order;
  `counts` gives `cached_count`, `missing_count` and `mismatch_count`, each
  equal to the number of entries with that status. The audit is computed on
  every read and never writes: no cache record is inserted, invalidated or
  repaired, so impact queries, impact paths and source paths behave exactly
  as before. The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters; any
  body bytes (whitespace-only included) or query parameter → `422`, and an
  unknown dataset or version → `404`, with `404` taking precedence over
  `422` as in the impact query.
- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-audit/repair`
  — controlled repair of the version's impact cache, appended one segment
  after the read-only audit address and accepting POST only. Every field of
  the version is recomputed against the committed lineage graph with the
  exact impact-query semantics: a field without a cache record gets one
  (`created`), a stored record that disagrees is rewritten (`updated`) and a
  matching record is left untouched (`unchanged`). Entries are sorted by
  field name ascending and the JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level
  keys `dataset`, `version`, `entries` and `counts` in that order; each
  entry has exactly `field` and `action`, and `counts` gives
  `created_count`, `updated_count` and `unchanged_count`. Written records
  are ordinary cache rows visible immediately to impact queries and
  surviving restarts; a subsequent audit reports every field as `cached`.
  The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters — any body
  bytes (whitespace-only included) or query parameter → `422`, an unknown
  dataset or version → `404` (with `404` taking precedence as in the audit),
  and concurrent repairs of the same version have a single winner, the
  loser receiving `409` and changing nothing. Every rejection writes
  nothing; lineage registrations and deletions, impact queries, path
  explanations, source-path reads and the read-only audit are unaffected.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact-paths?field=<field>` —
  read-only shortest-path explanation of the same impact, computed fresh on
  every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions, lineage
  mappings and the impact cache are never touched). The path and the `field`
  query parameter together name an existing field. The JSON document is
  deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
  newline) with top-level keys `source`, `impacts`, `direct_count` and
  `indirect_count` in that order; `source` is the start field reference
  (`{"dataset", "version", "field"}`). Each `impacts` entry has exactly the
  location keys `dataset`, `version`, `field`, then `path` and `path_length`;
  entries are deduplicated, never contain the source and are sorted by dataset,
  version and field ascending. `path` is the shortest node sequence from the
  source to the field, including both ends, and each node has the same
  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}` shape; `path_length` is the number of
  edges on the path (`1` for a direct downstream field, increasing for
  indirect ones). Among several shortest paths, the lexicographically smallest
  node sequence (compared by dataset, version and field) is chosen; cycles
  terminate. `direct_count` counts fields at distance 1 and `indirect_count`
  the fields farther away, and a field with no downstream returns an empty
  `impacts` array and both counts zero, never an error. The endpoint takes no
  request body and no query parameter other than `field` (a missing, blank or
  repeated `field` is likewise a `422`); unknown dataset/version/field →
  `404`, with `404` taking precedence over every `422` except that a repeated
  `field` is judged before the field lookup and is therefore always a `422`.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/source-paths?field=<field>` —
  read-only upstream companion of the lineage impact query, computed fresh on
  every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions, lineage
  mappings and the impact cache are never touched). The path and the `field`
  query parameter together name an existing field; the `field` value is
  matched literally (never trimmed), so a whitespace-padded name that matches
  no stored field is a `404`. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys
  `source`, `origins`, `direct_count`, `indirect_count` and
  `source_dataset_count` in that order; `source` is the start field reference
  (`{"dataset", "version", "field"}`). Each `origins` entry has exactly the
  location keys `dataset`, `version`, `field`, then `path` and `path_length`;
  entries are deduplicated, never contain the start field and are sorted by
  dataset, version and field ascending. An origin is a field whose mapping
  points (directly or transitively) at the start field. `path` is the
  shortest node sequence walking from the start field up to the origin,
  including both ends, and each node has the same
  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}` shape; `path_length` is the number of
  edges on the path (`1` for a direct source, increasing for indirect ones).
  Among several shortest paths, the lexicographically smallest node sequence
  (compared by dataset, version and field) is chosen; cycles terminate.
  `direct_count` counts origins at distance 1, `indirect_count` the origins
  farther away and `source_dataset_count` the distinct dataset names among
  all origins; a field with no sources returns an empty `origins` array and
  all counts zero, never an error. The endpoint takes no request body and no
  query parameter other than `field` (a missing, blank or repeated `field` is
  likewise a `422`); unknown dataset/version/field → `404`, with `404`
  taking precedence over every `422` except that a repeated `field` is judged
  before the field lookup and is therefore always a `422`.

  Impact results are cached persistently (they survive restarts) and every
  read reflects the currently committed lineage graph: creating a schema
  version invalidates the cache entries related to that dataset, and creating
  or deleting a lineage mapping invalidates the cached impacts of the
  mapping's source field and of every field that can reach it. Unrelated
  cache entries are preserved.

### Quality rules

Quality rules validate rows against a schema version. Rules are version-scoped
and persisted (including their enabled state) across restarts.

- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules` — create a rule.
  Body: `{"name": "id required", "kind": "not_null", "params": {...}}`. Returns
  `201` with `id`, `name`, `kind`, `params`, `enabled`, `created_at`; `enabled`
  defaults to `true`. Rule names must be unique within a version (`409` on
  conflict). Referenced dataset/version/field must exist (`404`); other invalid
  input returns `422` and nothing is written. Supported kinds:
  - `not_null` — params `{"field": "<existing field>"}`.
  - `numeric_range` — params `{"field": "<existing field>", "min": <finite
    number>, "max": <finite number>}` with `min <= max`.
  - `unique` — params `{"fields": ["<existing field>", ...]}`: a non-empty list
    of distinct, existing field names.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules` — list rules
  sorted by `id` ascending.
- `PATCH /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/{rule_id}` —
  enable or disable a rule. Body: `{"enabled": true}` (boolean only); returns
  the updated rule. Unknown rule/dataset/version → `404`.
- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluate` —
  evaluate rows. Body: `{"rows": [{...}, ...]}`. Only enabled rules run.
  Returns `{"dataset", "version", "results"}` with results sorted by `rule_id`;
  each result has `rule_id`, `name`, `passed` and `violations` (0-based row
  indices in ascending order).
  - `not_null` fails on missing or `null` values.
  - `numeric_range` fails on missing, `null`, non-numeric, boolean or
    out-of-range values (boundaries included).
  - `unique` compares the tuple of `fields` values per row; a missing field
    counts as `null`, and every row taking part in a duplicate group is a
    violation.
  - With an empty `rows` list every rule passes.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations` —
  list the persisted evaluation history of the version, ordered by `sequence`
  (occurrence order). Every successful evaluation appends one immutable
  summary (`sequence`, `dataset`, `version`, `row_count`,
  `violation_row_count` — the number of distinct submitted rows violating at
  least one rule — `results` and `created_at`); rejected or failed
  evaluations leave no record, and an empty `rows` submission is recorded
  with zero violations. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations/diff`
  — read-only diff between the two most recent recorded evaluations
  (`from_sequence` → `to_sequence`). `added_violation_rows` /
  `removed_violation_rows` are the 0-based row indices that started or
  stopped violating any rule, and each entry of `rules` carries the rule's
  `before`/`after` side (`violation_count` and `violations`), the per-rule
  `added_violations` / `removed_violations` and the numeric
  `violation_count_delta` (negative, zero or positive). A rule missing from
  one side (disabled or created between the two evaluations) has a `null`
  side and `null` row-level diff fields. With fewer than two recorded
  evaluations the response is an explicit empty result (null sequences,
  empty lists), not an error. Same `404`/`422` rules as the history
  endpoint; nothing is written.

### Quality anomaly detection

Anomaly detection runs over the persisted evaluation history of a schema
version. A version carries at most one detection config; scans append
immutable anomaly records that persist across restarts.

- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection`
  — register the version's detection config. The body contains exactly three
  integers: `consecutive_worsening_steps` (at least `2`),
  `violation_row_limit` and `rule_violation_limit` (both non-negative).
  Returns `201` with the config (`id`, `dataset`, `version`, the three
  thresholds, `created_at`). A second config for the same version returns
  `409`; unknown dataset/version → `404`; missing, extra, non-integer or
  out-of-range fields → `422` and nothing is written.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection`
  — return the registered config (`404` when none exists). The endpoint takes
  no request body and no query parameters (`422`).
- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection/scan`
  — run one detection pass over the persisted evaluation history and return
  the anomaly records this scan newly added (ordered by `id`); they are
  persisted in the same transaction. Scanning without a registered config
  returns `409`; an empty history is a successful scan that writes nothing.
  The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`). Each
  record has `id`, `kind`, `sequence` (the history sequence it points to),
  `rule_id`, `violation_count` and `created_at`; `kind` is one of:
  - `row_limit` — the evaluation's `violation_row_count` exceeds
    `violation_row_limit` (`rule_id` is `null`).
  - `rule_limit` — one rule's violation count in the evaluation exceeds
    `rule_violation_limit`; `rule_id` carries the rule's id.
  - `trend` — the violation row counts of adjacent evaluations strictly
    increase and the consecutive increase count at the tail of the history
    reaches `consecutive_worsening_steps`; the record points to the final
    evaluation of the increasing sequence (`rule_id` is `null`). A shorter
    run or any decline produces no trend record.

  A record with the same kind, history sequence and rule id is never
  duplicated: repeated scans only persist and return newly appearing
  anomalies, and concurrent scans store each anomaly exactly once with
  contiguous ids.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection/anomalies`
  — list every anomaly record of the version sorted by `id` ascending (empty
  when there are none, never an error). Same `404`/`422` rules as the scan
  endpoint; nothing is written.

### Quality gate

The quality gate is the release-readiness verdict of a schema version. It is
computed fresh from the persisted records on every read — nothing is cached,
re-run or written, and the rule definitions are never consulted (violations
recorded for rules since disabled still count).

- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/gate` — return the
  verdict as a deterministic JSON document (fixed key order, compact
  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline):
  `{"dataset", "version", "verdict", "reasons", "counts"}`.
  - `verdict` is one of:
    - `pass` — the latest recorded evaluation passed every rule and no
      anomaly record exists; a zero-violation evaluation left by an empty
      `rows` submission is a valid basis.
    - `undetermined` — no evaluation was ever recorded; `reasons` is empty
      and the read succeeds (never an error).
    - `fail` — the latest recorded evaluation still has violating rows, or
      the version carries any anomaly record.
  - `reasons` lists every factor that lowers the verdict, sorted by `kind`,
    `sequence` and `rule_id` (null ids first), all ascending. Each reason has
    `kind`, `sequence`, `rule_id` and `violation_count` (a missing rule id is
    `null`, never omitted). Every rule with violations in the latest
    evaluation contributes one `violation` reason with its violation row
    count; every persisted anomaly record contributes one reason of its own
    kind (`row_limit`, `rule_limit` or `trend`). A rule that appears in both
    yields two reasons — they are never merged or deduplicated.
  - `counts` reports how many persisted records the verdict examined:
    `evaluations`, `anomalies` and `reasons` (the length of the reason list).
  - The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters: any body
    bytes — including whitespace-only ones — or any query parameter are a
    `422`, checked after the path dataset/version resolves (`404` first).
    Nothing is written on any rejection.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/gate/at?timestamp=...`
  — the same verdict as it stood at a requested instant. `timestamp` must be
  a timezone-bearing ISO-8601 date-time; only evaluations and anomaly records
  written at or before it count, and the latest evaluation of that window is
  the one with the highest sequence inside it. The response is the same
  deterministic document as the bare gate (`dataset`, `version`, `verdict`,
  `reasons`, `counts`, one trailing newline), with the counts covering only
  the records inside the window. A window without any evaluation is
  `undetermined` with an empty reason list — a normal response, never an
  error. The endpoint accepts GET only and is strictly read-only. The path
  dataset/version resolves first (`404`); afterwards any request body bytes
  (whitespace-only included), a missing, repeated, unparseable or
  timezone-less `timestamp`, or any other query parameter are a `422` that
  writes nothing.

### Privacy policies

Privacy policies attach a sensitivity classification and masking strategy to a
single field of a schema version, enabling role-based de-identification of row
data. Policies (including their enabled state) are persisted across restarts.

- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies` — register a
  policy. Body:
  `{"field": "email", "classification": "PII", "masking": "partial", "allowed_roles": ["analyst"]}`.
  `field` must name an existing field of the version; `classification` is a
  non-empty string; `masking` is `redact` or `partial`; `allowed_roles` is an
  array of distinct, non-empty role names and may be empty. Returns `201` with
  the submitted fields plus `id`, `enabled` (defaults to `true`) and
  `created_at`. Registering two policies for the same field within one version
  returns `409`. Unknown dataset/version/field → `404`; other invalid input →
  `422` and nothing is written.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies` — list policies
  sorted by `id` ascending.
- `PATCH /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/{policy_id}` —
  enable or disable a policy. Body: `{"enabled": true}` (boolean only); returns
  the updated policy. Unknown policy/dataset/version → `404`.
- `PUT /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/{policy_id}` —
  revise a policy. Body carries exactly the three adjustable fields:
  `{"classification": "PII", "masking": "partial", "allowed_roles":
  ["analyst"]}`, using the same value rules as registration — a non-empty
  `classification` after trimming, `masking` of `redact` or `partial`, and an
  `allowed_roles` array of distinct, non-empty-after-trimming role names that
  may be empty. The three fields are replaced together from one whole
  submission. The revision never changes the policy id, the field it belongs
  to, its `enabled` state or its `created_at`; it writes only the policy
  itself — no policy is created, no identification record is touched and no
  masking suggestion is registered. Returns `200` with the updated policy in
  the same shape as the policy read, and the revision survives restarts. The
  next privacy view read (and every later masked read) judges each value by
  the revised classification, masking and allowed roles. Already-written
  masking-hit records, access records and cleanup requests are unaffected —
  their contents and ordering stay as written; the grouping of the summary,
  diff and reconciliation responses keeps the same counting rules, while the
  policy classification and masking reported on trend rows (and the policy
  entries of the coverage check and compliance export) reflect the current
  values. Advisory masking suggestions are unaffected. Unknown
  dataset/version/policy → `404`, judged before every request-shape check;
  missing or extra fields, a blank `classification`, an illegal `masking`
  value, duplicate or blank `allowed_roles` entries, an empty or
  whitespace-only body, malformed JSON, a non-object payload or any query
  parameter → `422` and nothing is written. Concurrent revisions of the same
  policy have exactly one winner; the loser receives `409` and changes no
  field.

- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view` — return a
  role-scoped, order-preserving copy of submitted rows. Body:
  `{"role": "guest", "rows": [{...}, ...]}` with a non-empty `role` and a list
  of row objects. Response: `{"dataset", "version", "rows"}`. Only enabled
  policies whose field appears in a row mask the value when `role` is not in
  `allowed_roles`:
  - `redact` replaces every non-`null` value with `"***"`.
  - `partial` keeps the first character and last two characters of strings
    longer than 4 characters (e.g. `"alice@example.com"` → `"aom"`); every other
    non-`null` value (short strings, numbers, booleans, …) is replaced with
    `"***"`.
  - `null` values and fields without a policy are returned unchanged; rows
    missing a covered field are left without it.

  Every successful view also appends one audit record per value it actually
  masked (the same field masked in several rows yields one record per masked
  value; a role in `allowed_roles`, a `null` value, an uncovered field or a
  disabled policy never hits); the records are persisted per version and are
  append-only.

  Every successful view additionally appends exactly one access record,
  whether or not it masked any value (an empty `rows` submission is recorded
  too). Rejected or failed views leave neither kind of record.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/access-records`
  — list every access record of the version, ordered by `sequence` ascending
  (empty when there are none, never an error). Each record has `sequence`,
  `role`, `row_count` (the number of submitted rows), `masked_count` (the
  number of masking-hit records the same view wrote, so the two logs
  cross-check) and `created_at`. The endpoint takes no request body and no
  query parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`. Nothing is
  written.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records`
  — list every masking-hit record of the version, ordered by `sequence`
  ascending (empty when there are none, never an error). Each record has
  `sequence`, `field`, `policy_id`, `role`, `masking` and `created_at`. The
  endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown
  dataset/version → `404`. Nothing is written.
- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/search`
  — read-only filtered retrieval of the same masking-hit records. The
